summary: This document extends the identifiers used in the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). Identifiers following IP/MPLS conventions already existed. This adds identifier formats typically used by the ITU-T for MPLS-TP management and Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions.

eli5.summary: Telephone-style networks and internet-style networks name things differently. This adds the telephone-style names so both groups can talk about the same equipment.

subtitle: Telephone-carrier-style names for MPLS-TP operators, tunnels, paths and OAM entities, as an alternative to IP-style ones.

tldr.problem: RFC 6370 names MPLS-TP operators and entities with IP/MPLS conventions, but ITU-T-style networks identify operators with ITU Carrier Codes instead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ICC_Operator_ID, a Country Code plus an ITU Carrier Code, that can replace the Global_ID, and it rebuilds the tunnel, LSP, pseudowire and maintenance identifiers on top of it.
tldr.outcome: Operators who follow ITU-T conventions get globally unique identifiers. The RFC defines only the identifiers, not how protocols carry them, and does not intend both kinds to be used in the same domain.

today: RFC 6923 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013, and the unit data show it has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC defines only identifiers, and leaves their use and any protocol extensions to carry them to other documents.

sections.title: Why a Second Naming Scheme
sections.content:
RFC 6370 defined identifiers for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP), covering nodes, interfaces, tunnels, label switched paths (LSPs), pseudowires and the entities used for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM). Those identifiers follow IP/MPLS conventions, and an operator is identified by a Global_ID based on its Autonomous System number.

RFC 6923 adds an alternative that follows ITU-T conventions. It is not intended that both kinds of identifier will be used at the same time in the same domain.

The scope is narrow. The RFC solely defines the identifiers. How they are used, and any protocol extensions to carry them, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: There were already name tags in one style. Companies from the telephone world use another style, so this adds those tags too, but you pick one style for a network.

sections.title: Notation Borrowed from RFC 6370
sections.content:
The identifiers are written with the notation from RFC 6370. Multi-word atomic identifiers use underscores, as in Node_ID. Identifiers made of other identifiers list them joined with double colons, as in Node_ID::IF_Num.

When the same identifier type appears more than once, a prefix and dash qualify it, so A1-Node_ID is the Node_ID of the node called A1. A1 marks the lower sort order and Z9 the higher. Groups of fields are wrapped in {...}.

The ordering is only a preferred one. Uniqueness depends on the uniqueness and scoping of the fields, and the ordering is not meant to constrain protocol designs.
sections.eli5: It is a way of writing a long address with pieces joined by double colons, where A1 and Z9 are just the two ends of a connection.

sections.title: The ICC_Operator_ID
sections.content:
The ITU-T identifies operators and service providers with an ITU Carrier Code (ICC), specified in ITU-T M.1400. The ITU-T Telecommunication Standardization Bureau keeps the list of assigned ICCs. National regulatory authorities act as intermediaries and make sure carrier codes are unique within their country.

An ICC is a string of one to six characters, each alphabetic (A-Z) or numeric (0-9). Alphabetic characters SHOULD be uppercase. To make it globally unique it is joined with a two-letter uppercase Country Code (CC) from ISO 3166-1. Both are coded according to ITU-T T.50. Together they form the ICC_Operator_ID, written CC::ICC.

The ICC_Operator_ID replaces the Global_ID, so Global_ID::Node_ID::IF_Num is functionally equivalent to ICC_Operator_ID::Node_ID::IF_Num. The same substitution applies to every identifier in RFC 6370 except the MEG, MEP and MIP identifiers, which are redefined.
sections.eli5: A country code plus a company code is like a phone number prefix, so no two companies in the world end up with the same name tag.

sections.title: Node, Interface, Tunnel, LSP and Pseudowire IDs
sections.content:
Node and interface identifiers keep their RFC 6370 shape. A Node_ID is a 32-bit value assigned by the operator, and zero is reserved and MUST NOT be used. An interface number, IF_Num, is a 32-bit unsigned integer, and 0 MUST NOT identify an MPLS-TP interface. An IF_ID is Node_ID::IF_Num, 64 bits, and is made globally unique by prefixing the ICC_Operator_ID.

A point-to-point tunnel ID is built from both end points' Node_IDs and a 16-bit Tunnel_Num at each end: A1-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::Z9-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}. For global uniqueness, the ICC_Operator_ID is added in front of each Node_ID.

LSP IDs extend the tunnel ID with a 16-bit LSP_Num. A co-routed bidirectional LSP is set up as one entity, so a single LSP_Num covers both directions. An associated bidirectional LSP needs a separate LSP_Num for each of its two unidirectional LSPs.

The pseudowire path ID has the same pattern, with an Attachment Individual Identifier of ICC_Operator_ID, Node_ID and AC_ID, where the AC_ID is defined in RFC 5003: A1-{ICC_Operator_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}::Z9-{ICC_Operator_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}.
sections.eli5: Each end of a connection gets a full address made of company, machine and a number, and the connection is named by writing both ends together.

sections.title: Maintenance Identifiers
sections.content:
For OAM, the RFC defines identifiers for entities described in RFC 6371. Unlike RFC 6370, it does not define separate ones for Sections, pseudowires and LSPs.

The MEG_ID (Maintenance Entity Group) is a string of up to 15 characters: the Country Code, the ICC, and a Unique MEG ID Code (UMC) defined by ITU-T, written CC::ICC::UMC. The UMC MUST start with the / character, which cannot appear in an ICC, so a short ICC followed by a UMC cannot be mistaken for a different split and a receiver can take the ID apart. The UMC MUST be unique within the organization identified by CC and ICC.

The MEP_ID (end point) is the MEG_ID followed by a 16-bit MEP_Index that is administratively assigned and MUST be unique within the MEG: MEG_ID::MEP_Index. It is globally unique because the MEG_ID is.

The MIP_ID (intermediate point) is a global IF_ID, the interface identifier prefixed with the ICC_Operator_ID. If only a per-node MIP model is used, one MIP is configured and its ID uses the Node_ID with an IF_Num of 0.
sections.eli5: Checkers who test a connection get tags too. The group tag says who owns it, and each checker adds a number so they can be told apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC extends an existing naming scheme and says it does not introduce new security concerns. It repeats the point from RFC 6370 that protocol specifications that use this naming scheme may bring security risks and questions about authenticating participants. Those specifications therefore need to describe the concerns and how to address them.
sections.eli5: A name tag alone is safe, but whatever rules use the tags must say how to stop people from pretending to be someone else.
